title: What is known about 1RB1RE_1LC0RF_1LA0LD_1LE1LC_0RA0LC_1RA---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RE_1LC0RF_1LA0LD_1LE1LC_0RA0LC_1RA---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The machine is a base-4 counter whose digits carry timers. Lean proves the sweep rule (one increment, any number of carries) for all values, and also that tapes of the same counter shape with short timers halt: so nonhalting cannot follow from the shape of the tape alone, it depends on the timer values the run from blank tape produces. An accelerated simulation that applies the rule in closed form and simulates every irregular sweep exactly reaches 102000 steps without a halt, never with more than one irregular pattern inside the counter at a time.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 68,700 cells have been visited and 26,681 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.523). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.092).

claims.title: The sweep rule, any number of carries
claims.text: At the left end in state C the tape is a^n0 s(d1) a^n1 ... s(dk) a^nk with a = 001 and separators s(0)=0, s(1)=011, s(2)=00, s(3)=0101. One sweep adds one to the base-4 number d1 d2 ...: for every n0 ≥ 2, every block ≥ 1 and every list of carried digits 3 (a list of any length), the carried digits become 0 and their blocks gain one a, and the first digit below 3 goes up by one (its block loses one a on 0→1 and 2→3).

claims.title: Exact step count without carry
claims.text: A sweep without carry takes 8·n0 + 6 steps (with carries, 8(n0+...+nj) + 10j + 6, checked by simulation).

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>2000</sup> steps
claims.text: py/accel.py applies t sweeps at once between irregular events (the counter plus t, each timer N_i = n_i + c(d_i) minus the wraps of its digit, the step count summed in closed form) and simulates every irregular sweep (overflow, fused digits) with an exact run-length simulator. From blank tape it reaches 102000 steps without a halt. It agrees with the plain simulator at every sweep start (checked up to 3·106 steps in Python and 3·108 with tools/c/tmrun.c), and the run-length simulator agrees with the plain one on random tapes.

claims.title: Only a small set of irregular patterns
claims.text: Up to 10300 steps only about twenty different irregular separator patterns appear after the simulated sweeps (two separators touching when a timer has run out, and the end 01 during overflow), each recurring many times, and there is never more than one irregular pattern inside the counter at a time (3,008 simulated sweeps with one, 2,405 with none).

claims.title: The same tape shape halts with short timers
claims.text: C> a^2 0 a^4 01 (one digit, block 4) halts at step 309,457 and C> a^43 0101 a^4 0101 a^4 01 (digits 3, 3, blocks 4, 4) at step 4,905,443. Both are sweep starts of exactly the counter form; the step counts agree with the accelerated simulator and a plain C simulator. A nonhalting proof must therefore use the timer values of the actual run.

claims.title: Many counter tapes with other timers halt
claims.text: All tapes with one or two digits, blocks 1..4 and n0 = 2..12: 136 halt within 10<sup>7</sup> steps. 300 random tapes with 2..7 digits and the block after digit i up to 4<sup>i+2</sup>: 22 halt within 10<sup>150</sup> steps, 20 of them at steps of 6 to 25 digits, one near 10<sup>52</sup> and one near 10<sup>89</sup>.

claims.title: A cryptid-like tail
claims.text: In the random runs the rate of halting falls off as the timers grow (a fusion of two digits is dangerous only when other timers run out in the same short window). The run from blank tape is far past the stage where most random runs halt; that it keeps surviving is likely, but nothing known forces it.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The only halting transition is F1; normal sweeps never reach it (proved). A halt needs several timers to run out close together, as in the short-timer tapes above; whether the run from blank tape ever produces such a coincidence is an open arithmetic question about its timers.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. Started on a blank tape, this machine counts in base 4: every sweep of its head adds one to a number written as separators between blocks of 001, and every digit carries a countdown timer. Lean proves the counting rule, and also that the same kind of tape halts when its timers are short; an accelerated simulation has followed the real run for 102000 steps without a halt.

facts.text: The sweep rule, for every value and any number of carries, proved in Lean.
Two tapes of the same counter shape with short timers halt (Lean).
No halt in the accelerated simulation (exact between and at irregular events).

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.523). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.092).
After 109 steps the tape spans 68,700 cells (51,976 left of the start, 61 right), with a density of 1s of 0.388.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: The tape is a base-4 number
html: Look at the tape each time the head is back at the left end in state C. It is made of blocks of the word a = 001 separated by one of four short words, and each separator is a base-4 digit:

separator0011000101
digit0123
So the tape reads C> a^n0 s(d1) a^n1 s(d2) a^n2 ... s(dk) a^nk 01, lowest digit first. From blank tape:

steptape at the left enddigits
447a5 0 a3 011 a3 010 1
493a6 011 a2 011 a3 011 1
547a7 00 a2 011 a3 012 1
609a8 0101 a1 011 a3 013 1
697a9 0 a2 00 a3 010 2 (a carry)
775a10 011 a1 00 a3 011 2

sections.heading: One sweep adds one
html: The head runs right over a^n0 (each 001 becomes 110 in state F), over every digit 3 and the block after it, turns at the first digit below 3 and runs back, restoring the as. The digits 3 become 0, the digit where it turned goes up by one. Each block left of that digit gains one a; the block right of it loses one when the digit goes 0→1 or 2→3. The sweep takes 8(n0 + ... + nj) + 10j + 6 steps for j carries.
Lean proves this for every value and any number of carries (sweep0..2 in lean/Rules.lean; the carried digits are a list of any length, crossed by induction).

So n0 grows by one a sweep, and for every other digit the number N = n + c(d), with c = 0, 1, 1, 2 for d = 0, 1, 2, 3, is constant except that it drops by one each time the digit wraps from 3 to 0, once every 4i sweeps for digit i. Every digit carries a timer.

sections.heading: Overflows and fused digits
html: Overflow. When every digit is 3 the carry runs into the end 01: the head crosses the whole tape and back, every digit becomes 0 and a new lowest digit appears whose block is the old a^n0; so its timer starts at n0 = 4k, with k the number of digits.
A timer runs out. When a block reaches 0 the separators on its two sides touch, and within a few cycles of the lower digit the two digits fuse into one:

steptape at the left end
5,622,078a112 0101 a999 0101 a123 00 a1 011 a50 0 a3 01
5,631,976a113 0 a1000 0 a124 0101011 a50 0 a3 01 (the block a1 is gone)
5,680,420a129 0 a996 0 a123 0 a1 00 a50 0 a3 01
5,730,766a145 0 a992 0 a122 01100 a50 0 a3 01
5,783,024a161 0 a988 0 a121 0000 a50 0 a3 01
5,837,194a177 0 a984 0 a120 010 a50 0 a3 01
5,890,7071010 a192 0 a980 0 a119 011 a49 0 a3 01 (two digits have become one)

A new digit gets the timer 4k but wraps 4k times in the next cycle alone, so most new digits soon fuse with a neighbour. The number of digits still grows, about 0.83 per factor 10 of the step count (248 digits at 10300 steps). The tape grows at the left end by three cells a sweep, which is the square-root side; the highest digits and the end sit right of the start and change only every 4k sweeps, the logarithmic side.

sections.heading: Why it is open
html: The only halting transition is F1, entered from B1. In a normal sweep F only reads the 0s of 001, so a halt could only come from an irregular sweep. The accelerated simulator applies the counter rule in closed form between irregular events and simulates each irregular sweep exactly; it reaches 102000 steps without a halt, and in that time only about twenty different irregular patterns occur, never more than one inside the counter at a time.
But the shape of the tape does not protect it. Tapes of exactly the counter form, with short timers, halt. Lean checks two by evaluation:

tapedigitshalts at step
C> a^2 0 a^4 010309,457
C> a^43 0101 a^4 0101 a^4 013 34,905,443

There several timers run out close together: two digits fuse while the blocks below them are short too, the fused patterns run into each other, and the counter collapses until the end 01 is eaten and B reads a 1 with another 1 after it. Of 300 random tapes with timers in the range the real run uses, 22 halt within 10150 steps, most of them early (steps of 6 to 25 digits), one near 1052 and one near 1089.

So a proof of nonhalting would need an arithmetic fact about the timers along the run from blank tape: that two of them never run out in the same dangerous window. Nobody has one. The behaviour is that of a cryptid: deterministic, with no visible reason to halt and no proof that it cannot.

summary: A base-4 counter (one digit per separator) whose digits carry countdown timers; timers that run out fuse digits. Sweep rule proved in Lean; the same tape shape halts with short timers (Lean); no halt in 10^2000 steps (accelerated simulation).
